Low-precision quantization packs multiple parallel channels per BRAM
This project introduces a novel software-hardware co-
design environment that interfaces an FPGA with a
microcontroller to enable real-time, edge-based comp-
uter vision without relying on cloud infrastructure. Within
are trained in PyTorch with quantized parameters, and
seamlessly transformed into an equivalent Verilog
itecture fully utilizes the FPGA's limited compute
resources (LCs, DSPs, BRAMs) to perform inference on a
binarized live input feed from the microcontroller. Finally,
design time is drastically reduced by profiling each
module's hardware overhead, generating all valid network
topologies, and ranking them based on highly accurate
compute dot products between the sliding window and weights.
- Combinational mode offers single-cycle latency, optimal for lower input bandwidth.
- Sequential mode trades DSP blocks and added latency to save Logic Cells (LC).
data movement is identical, but performs a max instead of dot product..
- Latency can be reduced by dividing the workload over multiple DSPs.
- PyTorch network mapped to Verilog, confirming it fits within FPGA hardware budget.

- [1] J. H. Lee et al., "Unifying block-wise PTQ and distillation-based QAT...", arXiv:2506.09104, 2025. [2] J. Choi et al., "PACT: Parameterized Clipping Activation for Quantized Neural Networks", arXiv:1805.06085, 2018.
Convolution LUT4 and FF Usage vs DSP Allocation
- Synthesized each module over all parameter combinations.
- Trained regression models to predict FF and LUT4 costs.
- Developed a constrained DFS to generate all real networks.
- Architectures that fully utilize logic cells perform better.
- Ternary activations allow for deeper networks, but gradients
vanish, with accuracy peaking at networks with three layers.
By integrating this network sweep and accuracy prediction
within an automated toolchain, designers can rapidly deploy
the globally optimal architecture for accuracy and throughput.
Benchmarking using the MNIST dataset yields real quantized
accuracy of 95% and 72 fps. This exact accuracy was
validated physically on the FPGA, and fully integrated for low-
power edge inference via the ESP32c3 and Arducam frontend.
